course.title: Reliability Engineering for AI Services
course.tagline: Set, measure and defend the reliability standards of an AI service: objectives, capacity, degraded modes, incidents, safe releases and verified models
course.description: Participants set and defend reliability standards for AI services that other teams build. For a fictional postal and parcels operator running a bilingual tracking assistant on a self-hosted open-weight model with retrieval, they write service level objectives for availability, latency and answer quality, set admission limits with headroom from measured goodput, design and chaos-test degradation paths, lead incident drills and blameless reviews, release through canaries with automated rollback, and admit models only after verifying signatures and bills of materials.
course.audience: Specialists. Engineers who have completed the level 300 core or can show equivalent work: a production AI system they built, operated and can defend.
prerequisites: AE-305 Operating Machine Learning and Language Model Systems
AE-307 Container Orchestration and Cloud Infrastructure for AI Workloads
Has written alerting rules on service metrics
Runs containers on a single-node cluster
Has released a service through a canary or blue-green rollout
Reads a goodput-versus-concurrency curve (the measurement method is taught in AE-401)

Setup: a laptop CPU with uv, or Google Colab. Nothing downloads a model; the self-hosted engine is a calibrated simulator and the answers are recorded. Run 00_setup_check before Day 1; see labs/README.md.
course.format_note: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task

outcomes.text: Design service level objectives for availability, latency and answer quality, with error budgets and a release policy, given a month of synthetic telemetry and a sampled online quality signal
outcomes.evidence: an objectives document defended against a reviewer's challenges

outcomes.text: Decide an admission limit and shedding priorities that keep headroom for the busiest hour, given the self-hosted model, a recorded traffic trace and the service objectives
outcomes.evidence: a justified operating point and margin, and an overload replay in which priority traffic still meets its objective

outcomes.text: Design degradation for overload and dependency failure using load shedding, a smaller fallback model and a cached-answer mode, given overload, retrieval outage and provider timeout scenarios
outcomes.evidence: chaos test results showing each path keeps the minimum service, with quality measured in each mode

outcomes.text: Lead an incident drill from detection to recovery and write a blameless review, given a silent quality regression after a model update
outcomes.evidence: a timeline, a decision log, owned corrective actions and a new regression test

outcomes.text: Build a release gate that verifies model signatures, a bill of materials and licences before deployment, given signed, tampered and unlicensed model artefacts
outcomes.evidence: a pipeline run that admits the valid artefact and rejects the others, with logs

outcomes.text: Review another team's AI service for production readiness and set launch conditions, given a peer's service, its telemetry and a readiness checklist
outcomes.evidence: ranked findings and a launch decision defended before a panel

case_study.name: Rasael Post and Parcels
case_study.summary: Rasael Post and Parcels is a fictional national postal and parcels operator whose bilingual assistant, Athar, answers tracking, redelivery and help questions on a self-hosted open-weight model with retrieval over 3,000 Arabic and English help articles. Participants set its objectives, decide its admission limit, design and chaos-test its degraded modes, run an incident drill on a silent quality regression, release through a canary, and admit models only after verifying signatures and bills of materials; all telemetry, traffic, answers, incidents and model artefacts are synthetic and generated with a fixed seed.

days.label: Day 1
days.title: Objectives that match what users need
days.subtitle: Indicators and objectives for latency, availability and answer quality, sliced by language

sessions.label: Session 1
sessions.title: AI services fail differently
sessions.summary: An AI service can be up, fast on a probe and still wrong, slow or silent for its users
outcomes: Name four ways an AI service fails while an uptime check stays green
Read per-minute telemetry by language and by mode
Separate what users felt from what the probe measured

lab.title: What the uptime check missed
lab.summary: Read a week of Athar telemetry and list the incidents an uptime check would miss, with their duration and the indicator that shows each one.

steps.text: Load the week and plot requests, probe and errors
Find the minutes where the probe was green and users were not
Group them into incidents with a start, a duration and a signal
Name the indicator that would have caught each one

lab.stretch: Repeat the search for Arabic and English separately and compare

sessions.label: Session 2
sessions.title: Indicators for latency and quality
sessions.summary: Indicators as good events over valid events: first-token time, per-token time, availability and a sampled quality grade
outcomes: Define an indicator as good events over valid events
Exclude probes and client cancellations with a written reason
Estimate a sampled quality rate with its interval, by language

lab.title: Four indicators from one day
lab.summary: Define first-token time, per-token time, availability and a sampled quality grade on a day of request logs, with the exclusions written down and quality sliced by language with an interval.

steps.text: Read the request log and its fields
Write the valid-event filter and its exclusions
Latency indicators: first token and per token
Availability as good over valid requests
Quality grade by language, with a 95% interval

lab.stretch: How many graded samples per day would narrow the Arabic interval to two points?

sessions.label: Session 3
sessions.title: Objectives and error budgets
sessions.summary: Objectives tied to what users need, the budget they leave, and a release policy that spends it
outcomes: Set an objective from a user task, not from last month
Compute budget burn over a month and per week
Write a release policy that decides from the remaining budget

lab.title: Objectives, budget and release policy
lab.summary: Set objectives for Athar, compute the budget burned over a supplied month and write the release policy that decides five pending release requests.

steps.text: Write the four objectives with their windows
Compute the budget and what the month burned
Find the week that burned most and why
Write the release policy and decide five requests

lab.stretch: Add a policy line for a budget spent by a dependency, not by a release

sessions.label: Session 4
sessions.title: Objectives for multi-step tasks
sessions.summary: A booking flow succeeds per task, not per call: completion, cost per completed task and escalation
outcomes: Explain why per-call success hides failed tasks
Define completion, cost and escalation indicators for a flow
Set objectives a flow can be held to

lab.title: Indicators for the redelivery flow
lab.summary: Define completion, cost and escalation indicators for the redelivery booking flow from 2,000 recorded sessions, and show what per-call success hides.

steps.text: Read the sessions and their steps
Per-call success against per-task completion
Cost per completed booking, with the loops
Escalation rate and objectives for the flow

lab.stretch: Find the step where most abandoned sessions stop

days.label: Day 2
days.title: Capacity and failure
days.subtitle: Admission limits from measured goodput, degraded modes and chaos experiments

sessions.label: Session 1
sessions.title: Capacity with headroom
sessions.summary: Goodput falls past a concurrency the engine can sustain; the operating point leaves headroom for the busiest hour
outcomes: Read tail latency and goodput from a concurrency sweep
Choose an operating point and justify it against the objectives
Size replicas for the busiest hour with a stated margin

lab.title: Goodput curve and operating point
lab.summary: Load-test the simulated self-hosted engine at rising concurrency, find where goodput falls, set the operating point and size the replicas for the busiest hour with a margin.

steps.text: Run one load step and read its latencies
Sweep concurrency and compute goodput
Find the knee and choose the operating point
Replicas and margin for the busiest hour

lab.stretch: Repeat the sweep with long prompts and see the knee move

sessions.label: Session 2
sessions.title: Admission control and shedding
sessions.summary: Admit what the engine can serve, queue little, shed the least important traffic first
outcomes: Set a concurrency cap from the operating point
Rank traffic into priority classes with a reason
Show by replay that priority traffic keeps its objective

lab.title: A cap and priority shedding
lab.summary: Add a concurrency cap and three priority classes in front of the engine, then replay the overload trace and check that priority traffic still meets its objective.

steps.text: Replay the overload trace with no admission control
Add the concurrency cap and a bounded queue
Add priority classes and shed from the lowest
Check each class against its objective

lab.stretch: Shed by deadline: drop a queued request that can no longer meet its objective

sessions.label: Session 3
sessions.title: Degraded modes
sessions.summary: A smaller fallback model and a cached-answer mode keep a minimum service; each one is measured and disclosed
outcomes: Design degraded modes with entry and exit conditions
Measure answer quality in each mode by language

lab.title: Fallback model and cached answers
lab.summary: Configure a smaller fallback model and a cached-answer mode, route by health signals, measure quality in each mode by language and keep personal tracking answers out of the cache.

steps.text: Grade the full mode on the question set
Grade the fallback model by language
Build the cached-answer mode and its refusal rule
Route by health signals and disclose the mode

lab.stretch: Set the cache freshness limit from how often help articles change

sessions.label: Session 4
sessions.title: Chaos experiments
sessions.summary: A hypothesis, a blast radius and an abort condition; failures that retries make worse
outcomes: Write a chaos experiment as a falsifiable hypothesis
Inject dependency failures and measure the minimum service
Stop a retry storm with a retry budget and backoff

lab.title: Outage, timeout and retry storm
lab.summary: Inject a retrieval outage, a provider timeout and a retry storm into the simulated service and check that the minimum service holds in each.

steps.text: Write the hypothesis and the minimum service

Provider timeout: does the fallback take over?

lab.stretch: Run the three faults at once and say which mode the users get

days.subtitle: Burn-rate alerts on quality, incident leadership, canaries and blameless learning

lab.title: A burn-rate alert on quality

Two windows and two burn rates

lab.title: Game day: a model-update regression

steps.text: Read the roles and the first page
Detect and declare: first decisions
Mitigate: choose and apply the action
Personal data in answers: the breach decision
Close and hand over the log

lab.stretch: Rerun the drill with a different first action and compare time to mitigate

Timeline and contributing factors

days.label: Capstone
days.title: Readiness review defences
days.subtitle: A production readiness review defended before a panel, with a live fault to diagnose

capstone.summary: A production readiness review of a peer's or a supplied AI service, covering objectives, capacity, degradation, incidents and release integrity with measured evidence in a public repository, defended before a panel of experienced engineers. The follow-up task applies one reliability standard to a service in the participant's own team or an open-source deployment
capstone.submission: A public GitHub repository link: the readiness review (objectives, capacity, degradation, incident drill, release integrity) with its measured evidence, logs and commit history
